questions.prompt: Explain what a key path is in Swift. In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how you create and read one, and why it is safer than Objective-C string KVC.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a key path is a strongly typed reference to a property created with backslash syntax
Notes that it is read via subscript and checked at compile time, avoiding runtime crashes from string typos

questions.modelAnswer: A key path in Swift is a first-class, strongly typed reference to a property created using backslash syntax like \Person.name. You read or write the referenced property using the instance subscript person[keyPath: path]. Unlike Objective-C string-based Key-Value Coding, Swift key paths are verified at compile time. Typos or type mismatches are caught before the app runs.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between KeyPath, WritableKeyPath, and ReferenceWritableKeyPath in Swift. Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that KeyPath is read-only, while WritableKeyPath allows reading and writing mutable properties on value types
Explains that ReferenceWritableKeyPath allows modifying mutable properties on reference classes

questions.modelAnswer: KeyPath provides read-only access to a property, which is used for constants or read-only computed properties. WritableKeyPath provides read and write access to mutable properties on value types, requiring a mutating context. ReferenceWritableKeyPath provides read and write access to mutable properties on reference types (classes). It allows mutating properties even on let constants because of reference semantics.

questions.prompt: How does Swift support key paths as functions? In 2 to 5 sentences, describe how this improves code readability in higher-order functions like map and filter.

rubric.criterion: Explains that Swift allows \Root.Value key paths to be passed wherever a closure of type (Root) -> Value is expected
Describes how this simplifies higher-order functions by replacing verbose closures with concise syntax like users.map(\.name)

questions.modelAnswer: Swift automatically converts key paths into functions of type (Root) -> Value wherever a matching closure is expected. Instead of writing verbose closures like users.map { $0.name }, developers can write users.map(\.name). This syntax improves code readability and reduces noise in functional pipelines. The compiler checks property types and accessibility during compilation.

questions.prompt: What is @dynamicMemberLookup in Swift, and how does it use key paths to provide type-safe proxy access? Answer in 2 to 5 sentences.
questions.lessonSection: How to answer in the interview

rubric.criterion: Explains that @dynamicMemberLookup allows types to handle arbitrary member access through subscript(dynamicMember:)
Notes that using KeyPath parameters ensures member lookups are verified at compile time with autocomplete and type safety

questions.modelAnswer: The @dynamicMemberLookup attribute allows types to forward property access dynamically through a custom subscript(dynamicMember:). When this subscript accepts a KeyPath parameter, Swift ensures all forwarded property accesses are checked at compile time. This allows wrapper types to expose properties of their underlying wrapped objects with full code completion and strict type safety.

rubric.criterion: Mentions using key paths in List or ForEach to specify unique identifiers (e.g. id: \.id)
Mentions using key paths with dynamic member lookup to project nested bindings ($state.user.name) or environment values

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI uses key paths extensively across its architecture. In collection views like List and ForEach, key paths provide unique identity extraction using the id parameter, such as id: \.id. Additionally, SwiftUI's Binding type uses @dynamicMemberLookup with key paths. This allows developers to project child bindings cleanly, such as writing $model.user.name.
